newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan says President Lee to seek U.S. transit.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan says President Lee to seek U.S. transit.

text.p: Taiwan said on Monday it would ask the United States to grant its president a transit visa -- and counted on approval from Washington despite an expected protest from arch rival China.

Foreign ministry spokesman Roy Wu said Taipei would seek a transit visa for President Lee Teng-hui at "an appropriate time" for Lee's first footfall on U.S. soil since his 1995 visit to New York that drew a furious response from Beijing.
"We believe that, based on friendly relations and open communication channels between the two sides (Taipei and Washington), there shouldn't be any problems," Wu told reporters.

The United States, which does not maintain official ties with Taiwan, said in April that Lee was eligible for a visa to transit Hawaii or the U.S. west coast on his way to a September conference in Panama.
But U.S. semi-official representatives in Taiwan said no request had been received as of Monday.
A senior Taiwan official told Reuters recently that the U.S. would "undermine its own sovereignty if it allows Beijing to dictate how it polices its own boundaries."

Beijing, which regards Nationalist-ruled Taiwan as a rebel province and seeks to isolate its leaders from the international arena, exploded in fury in June 1995 after Washington allowed Lee to visit his alma mater, Cornell University.
Beijing also has protested the many instances where Taiwan's vice president, foreign minister and other high officials have been granted U.S. visitors' or transit visas.
Wu said his ministry expected another loud protest from Beijing immediately after Washington grants the transit visa for Lee.
Taiwan's presidential office has declined to comment on planning for Lee's Panama trip.

Panama, one of just 30 states that recognise Taiwan's exiled Republic of China rather than the communist People's Republic in Beijing, has invited Lee to attend a September 7-10 conference for users of the Panama Canal Zone.

With many heads of state expected to attend the conference, diplomatically estranged Taiwan sees the forum as a rare chance for Lee to rub shoulders with world leaders -- though likely not with President Bill Clinton, who reportedly does not plan to attend.
Most air routes linking East Asia to Central America include stopovers on the U.S. west coast or Hawaii. Taiwan officials say privately that Lee's route would be no exception.
In June 1995, the United States sparked a crisis in China's already strained U.S. and Taiwan ties by granting Lee a visa to make a nominally private visit to Cornell in New York state.
Beijing responded furiously by temporarily downgrading its U.S. ties and freezing what up to then had been slowly warming semi-official talks with Taipei.

More chillingly, Beijing launched what became nine months of massive, menacing war games near Taiwan, including the firing of unarmed ballistic missiles into target zones just outside the capitalist island's two main ports.

Making no secret of its intentions, Beijing said the drills aimed to stifle a growing pro-independence mood on Taiwan, which it has seen as a rebel-held province since the Nationalist republic and army fled there in 1949 after losing China's civil war.
Though Beijing and Taipei agree on little, both officially espouse a common goal of eventual national reunification.
But Beijing insists this be under communist sovereignty and Taipei says union is possible only under multiparty democracy.
